title: TypeScript Fundamentals: Types, Unions, and Generic Collections
description: Learn how TypeScript adds static checking to JavaScript, model object shapes, narrow uncertain values, and use types that make common data transformations safer.
learningOutcomes: Explain the difference between TypeScript's static checking and JavaScript runtime behavior.
Use annotations and inference for common primitive and object values.
Explain why unknown is safer than any and narrow values before using them.
Model objects with interface and type aliases, including optional and union properties.
Use generics such as Array<T> to preserve the relationship between input and output types.
Model a typed user list and write functions that search, update, and filter it safely.
Derive create, preview, and patch types with utility types while separating static checking from runtime validation.
Explain what strict TypeScript compiler settings check and why they do not validate data at runtime.

blocks.text: TypeScript checks your program before it runs

TypeScript extends JavaScript with a static type system. The type checker analyzes code during development or build time to identify many mistakes before the program executes. Type annotations and interfaces are mostly erased from the emitted JavaScript: the browser or Node runs JavaScript, not TypeScript type declarations. TypeScript cannot prove every runtime behavior safe, and external data can still violate the type you hoped to receive.

blocks.prompt: What does setting `"strict": true` in tsconfig.json do?

options.text: Enables a family of stricter compile-time checks, including checks such as `noImplicitAny` and `strictNullChecks`.
options.feedback: Correct. The strict option enables related static checks that help detect unsafe assumptions; the flag itself does not change emitted JavaScript runtime behavior.

options.text: Adds runtime validators that reject any API payload that violates an interface.
options.feedback: TypeScript interfaces are erased at runtime. Use a runtime schema or explicit validation for untrusted API data.

options.text: Changes TypeScript into a different browser runtime and leaves types in the output.
options.feedback: Browsers still run JavaScript; TypeScript type declarations are normally erased from emitted JavaScript.

options.text: Turns off compiler errors so an application can build even when types are inconsistent.
options.feedback: Strict mode generally enables more checks, so it can surface additional issues rather than suppress them.

blocks.explanation: The `strict` option enables a family of static type-checking rules. It improves diagnostics at compile time but does not replace runtime validation of network, storage, or user-provided data.

blocks.title: Types describe what code may assume
blocks.text: A type is a contract for values at a point in the program. Good types make assumptions explicit, guide editor tooling, and help refactoring. They are not runtime validation by themselves, so parse or validate data from APIs, storage, user input, and other untrusted boundaries.
Annotations and inference

A type annotation explicitly states the allowed type, such as let count: number = 0. Type inference lets TypeScript determine the type from an initializer or surrounding context, so you do not need to annotate every local variable. Add annotations where they clarify a public contract, a function boundary, or an ambiguous value; avoid duplicating obvious information without a benefit.

blocks.caption: Primitive annotations and inferred values

blocks.text: Type function inputs and outputs

Function parameter types constrain which arguments callers may pass. The return type describes what a successful call returns; TypeScript can often infer it, but explicit return types can clarify reusable APIs. A function that intentionally returns nothing can use void as its return type. Avoid using any to silence errors: that removes many checks from the expression and any values derived from it.
unknown versus any

any disables type checking for that value and allows most operations without proof. unknown also accepts any incoming value, but it requires you to check or narrow the value before using it as a more specific type. Prefer unknown at boundaries where a value's shape is not yet known, then validate it. A type assertion changes what the compiler assumes; it does not inspect or convert the runtime value.

steps.title: Accept an uncertain value safely
steps.explanation: unknown tells callers that the function can receive values of different types, while preventing the body from using the value arbitrarily.

steps.title: Narrow by checking the runtime type
steps.explanation: Within this branch, typeof value === 'string' narrows value to string, so string methods are available.

steps.title: Handle another supported type
steps.explanation: The number check narrows value to number, allowing toFixed. Each branch uses the value only after establishing the necessary fact.

steps.title: Make unsupported values explicit
steps.explanation: Values that are not strings or numbers reach the fallback. In real data parsing, decide whether to reject, report, or handle additional cases.

blocks.text: Model object shapes with interface and type

An interface describes an object shape and is often a good choice for domain entities such as User or Product. A type alias can name object shapes too, but can also describe unions, intersections, and other types. The two overlap for many object declarations; choose based on the required composition and conventions rather than assuming one is always superior.

steps.title: Define required properties
steps.explanation: id and name are required strings. role is a union of two exact string literals, so arbitrary strings are not allowed.

steps.title: Mark an optional property
steps.explanation: email?: string means the property can be absent. If present, its value must be a string unless other compiler options or a different declaration say otherwise.

steps.title: Check an object against the contract
steps.explanation: The object has the required fields and a valid role. It can omit email because that property is optional.

steps.title: Describe the required and optional fields
steps.explanation: The interface makes each field's type explicit. The category union limits the allowed strings, while description may be omitted.

steps.title: Create a value that satisfies Product
steps.explanation: The object supplies the required fields and a valid category. TypeScript checks this shape at compile time; it does not validate arbitrary JSON at runtime.

blocks.text: Union types and narrowing

A union type says a value may be one of several alternatives. For example, string | number represents either a string or a number. Code may use only operations valid for all alternatives until a condition narrows the union. Narrowing can use typeof, equality comparisons, the in operator, discriminant properties, or custom type guards. It is how TypeScript turns an uncertain contract into a usable specific value.

blocks.caption: A union forces the code to account for both cases

blocks.text: Generics preserve relationships between types

A generic parameter lets code work with a family of types while preserving information about the particular type used for one call. Array<T> means an array of T values. A function such as first<T>(items: T[]): T | undefined keeps its result tied to the element type: passing User[] yields User | undefined, not an unrelated any value.

steps.title: Introduce a type parameter
steps.explanation: T stands for the element type chosen for a particular call. The function is reusable without discarding the relationship to that type.

steps.title: Represent the empty-array case
steps.explanation: An array can be empty, so items[0] may be undefined. The return type makes that possibility explicit to every caller.

steps.title: Infer T from each call
steps.explanation: The first array contains strings, so the result is string | undefined. The second contains numbers, so its result is number | undefined.

steps.title: Keep item, predicate and result types connected
steps.explanation: The same T describes each input item and each returned item. The predicate decides whether an item is included.

steps.title: Use the helper with a concrete domain type
steps.explanation: The filter can work with Product or another type without losing the specific result type.

steps.title: Inspect the inferred result
steps.explanation: The result remains Product[]. This helper does not improve on Array.filter's built-in typing; it demonstrates how a generic API preserves a type relationship.

blocks.text: A practical typed user list

A useful type model makes everyday collection operations safer. If the array is User[], then filter callbacks receive User, find returns User | undefined, and a function that creates an updated user should preserve the remaining properties. Types help catch accidental property typos and invalid role values, but they do not validate arbitrary JSON at runtime.

blocks.caption: Filter and update a typed collection

blocks.title: Static types do not validate JSON at runtime
blocks.text: Typing fetch(...).json() as User[] only tells TypeScript what you want to assume; it does not prove the server sent valid User objects. Use runtime validation when data crosses a trust boundary. This project already uses Zod for validating structured lesson content and curriculum JSON.

blocks.prompt: What is the key safety difference between unknown and any?

options.text: unknown requires narrowing before type-specific operations
options.feedback: unknown accepts an uncertain value but makes the program check its type before using type-specific properties or methods.

options.text: unknown automatically converts values to strings
options.feedback: Neither unknown nor a type annotation converts a runtime value; explicit conversion or validation is needed.

options.text: any is safer because it reports every invalid operation
options.feedback: any disables many checks, so invalid operations can pass type checking.

options.text: unknown can only represent null and undefined
options.feedback: unknown can hold values of any runtime type; the restriction is on using it before narrowing.

blocks.explanation: unknown preserves safety by requiring evidence about the value's type before specific operations are allowed.

blocks.prompt: A TypeScript type assertion such as value as User validates that the runtime object has all properties declared by User.

options.text: True
options.feedback: A type assertion affects the compiler's assumption; it does not inspect or validate the runtime object.

options.text: False
options.feedback: Runtime validation requires checking the actual data, with code or a validation library; a type assertion alone is erased.

blocks.explanation: Compile-time type information does not automatically prove external data matches the type at runtime.

blocks.prompt: Which statements about TypeScript types are correct? Select all that apply.

options.text: An optional property may be absent from the object
options.feedback: The ? modifier marks the property as optional.

options.text: A union type may describe more than one allowed alternative
options.feedback: A union such as string | number represents either alternative, and code can narrow it before using specific operations.

options.text: A generic always means the runtime function creates a new class
options.feedback: Generics describe relationships between types and do not automatically create runtime classes or objects.

options.text: TypeScript type declarations normally remain in emitted browser JavaScript
options.feedback: Type-only syntax is erased during compilation, leaving JavaScript for the runtime.

blocks.explanation: Types describe allowed values and relationships at compile time; they are not a general runtime object system.

items: TypeScript adds static checking but compiles to JavaScript for the runtime.
Inference avoids unnecessary annotations; add explicit types at important contracts and boundaries.
unknown is safer than any because it requires narrowing before specific operations.
Use interface/type to model shapes, unions for alternatives, optional fields for absence, and generics to preserve type relationships.
Types do not validate external JSON by themselves; validate data at runtime when it crosses a trust boundary.

blocks.text: Deep dive: narrowing, discriminated unions, and runtime trust boundaries

TypeScript checks relationships between values at build time, but its types are erased from emitted JavaScript. A type annotation or `as User` cannot validate a payload received from a server. Treat external input as `unknown`, inspect it at runtime, and only then expose a trusted domain type. Discriminated unions let the compiler narrow the allowed fields for each state and can make unhandled cases visible.

steps.title: Use a discriminant to connect state and data
steps.explanation: Every union member has a status literal. Only success carries data and only error carries message, so callers cannot accidentally access fields that do not exist for the current state.

steps.title: Let control flow narrow the type
steps.explanation: The switch on status narrows state to a specific union member in each case. The compiler can see that state.message exists in the error branch.

steps.title: Make missing cases obvious
steps.explanation: assertNever accepts only never. If a new status is added and the switch is not updated, the supposedly exhaustive call stops type-checking.

blocks.title: Types disappear at runtime
blocks.text: This is not validation: `const user = payload as User`. It changes the compiler's belief, not the payload. For network data, parse from `unknown` with a runtime schema or explicit guards that check the fields the application actually uses.

steps.title: Accept unknown at an untrusted boundary
steps.explanation: unknown forces the implementation to prove the properties it uses. The first guard rejects null and non-object values.

steps.title: Validate each required property
steps.explanation: The shape is checked before constructing the trusted User result. Larger payloads should use a maintained schema validator rather than a long hand-written chain of checks.

steps.title: Return the application contract
steps.explanation: The returned object contains only the validated fields expected by this example; extra server properties are not automatically trusted.

blocks.prompt: What does `const user = payload as User` guarantee at runtime when payload comes from an HTTP response?

options.text: It verifies that payload has numeric id and string name
options.feedback: A type assertion is erased during compilation and does not inspect the response at runtime.

options.text: It tells the compiler to treat the expression as User without validating the actual value
options.feedback: The payload may still be malformed. Use runtime validation at external boundaries.

options.text: It converts the JSON value to a class instance
options.feedback: A TypeScript assertion does not transform or instantiate a value.

options.text: It removes all extra keys from payload
options.feedback: Assertions do not change object contents.

blocks.explanation: Static type checking and runtime validation solve related but different problems.

blocks.text: Utility types transform shapes at compile time

Partial<T>, Required<T>, Pick<T, K>, Omit<T, K>, and Readonly<T> derive a new static shape from an existing type. They reduce repetition when a domain model and an API payload share fields, but they do not create runtime validators or clone/freeze objects. Use the derived type at a boundary only when its meaning matches the actual operation.

steps.title: Start from the domain model
steps.explanation: Article describes the complete in-memory shape. A create request omits fields generated by the server; a preview needs only a selected subset.

steps.title: Derive narrower operation-specific types
steps.explanation: Omit removes selected keys, Pick keeps only selected keys, and Partial makes each remaining property optional. The intersection keeps id required in a patch.

steps.title: Check what the compiler accepts
steps.explanation: A patch can contain only id and changed fields. These types disappear from JavaScript output and do not validate JSON received from a server.

blocks.title: Optional is not nullable, and Partial is shallow
blocks.text: With strictNullChecks, an optional property may be absent (and when read may be undefined); it is not automatically a promise that null is valid. Partial changes only top-level properties, and Readonly is a compile-time restriction rather than Object.freeze. Validate untrusted values at runtime and define nested patch semantics deliberately.

options.text: It removes id from every JavaScript object and makes other properties optional at runtime.
options.feedback: Utility types do not rewrite objects; they are erased during compilation.

options.text: It validates an incoming JSON patch before the request is sent.
options.feedback: Static types do not validate external data; add a runtime schema or explicit checks.

options.text: At compile time, it describes an object with no id property and optional top-level fields from Article except id.
options.feedback: Correct. It changes only the type-level shape; runtime validation and nested semantics remain separate.

options.text: It deeply makes every nested property optional and immutable.
options.feedback: Partial is shallow, and it does not imply Readonly.

blocks.explanation: Utility types express compile-time transformations only. They neither mutate values nor validate network payloads.

blocks.prompt: Which TypeScript utility type makes every property of an existing object type optional?

options.text: `Partial<T>` makes each property of T optional in the resulting type.
options.feedback: Correct. Partial is a compile-time mapped utility type. It does not change the object or add runtime validation.

options.text: `Omit<T, K>` makes every property optional and keeps all keys.
options.feedback: Omit removes selected keys K from the resulting type; it does not make remaining properties optional.

options.text: `Pick<T, K>` makes each property optional and keeps the whole type.
options.feedback: Pick selects a subset of keys K from a type; the optional modifier is what Partial adds.

options.text: `Record<K, V>` marks all properties from an existing type as optional.
options.feedback: Record constructs a type with keys K and values V. It does not transform an existing type's properties to optional.

blocks.explanation: `Partial<T>` makes every property in T optional at the type level. It does not modify runtime values or validate external data.

items: Use unknown at external boundaries and validate before trusting a domain type.
Discriminated unions connect a state tag to the fields that are valid for that state.
Use exhaustive checks so new variants cause a compiler-visible follow-up rather than a silent runtime gap.
Use utility types to derive operation-specific API shapes, then validate external values at runtime.
